text: The next thing I wanted to chat about is what a harness is.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Harness is typically like a layer that wraps around the model that helps you make these tool calls in a loop to get you the outcome for the task at hand.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And it's making assumptions about what the model cannot do and trying to sort of fill those gaps.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So it's running in a loop, making tool calls, managing your context, encapsulating everything that the model cannot do.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: A good example is our Sonnet 4.5 model had something what we called context anxiety.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So whenever Sonnet 4.5 felt like you were getting to the end of the context limit, it would try to wrap up the task really quickly.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So when you're building a harness around Sonnet 4.5, you would add something like a context reset to get around the limitation of anxiety.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: But with the next model like Opus 4.5, Opus 4.5 did not have this limitation, and you did not need to do this context reset for Opus 4.5.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So when you're building a harness, you want to encapsulate all these assumptions for different models and keep up with it with every new model that comes up, which is why building a good harness is really, really important, and that's something we've tried to do with Cloud Managed Agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And then the last bit, you want your agent to have access to a sandbox or a computer, essentially a place where it's going to run the code it's writing to execute the task.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So typically you're giving Claude access to like a sandbox or a container where it's executing the code it's writing, it's able to edit files, install dependencies, et cetera.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Claude Code is a really good example of this.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: It's a horn essentially running locally on your computer, has access to your files, and it's executing, updating your files as it goes.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: It's also writing code that's untrusted.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: It might be buggy, so you want to make sure when you're deploying production agents, the code your agents are writing is sandboxed and contained within a container.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And then you want your sandbox to be isolated and the blast radius to be limited.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So typically you want to execute every task in a separate container so you're not mixing up and you're not increasing the blast radius for your tasks.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Next up, I'll walk you through the first architecture that we actually built managed agents with.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: This was in December of last year where we shipped our first architecture to our early access customers, got a bunch of feedback, and then actually pivoted to a new architecture.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So I'm going to walk you through some of the pitfalls and issues that we saw with the first one.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So with the first architecture, what we did was we put everything in the container.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So we had the session log of everything that's happened within that session.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So that session is essentially your unit of work.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: The harness was also running inside the container.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And then the sandbox execution was also happening inside the container.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: The benefit of that was because everything was in the container, there was no service boundaries to design for.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Everything was local, easy to edit.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: File edits were essentially just like syscalls.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: But what happened was we realized we adopted a pet.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So if you've not heard about the pet and cattle analogy from the old infrastructure days, pet is when you essentially have a named and hand-tended entity.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: When it gets sick, you have to nurture it back to life.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Otherwise, you basically cannot afford to lose it.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And cattle is more interchangeable, more disposable.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So when one fails, you can replace it with another one and move on.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So a good example is imagine you had like a single database shard.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: It goes down, your product is down, you have a pet.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: But imagine you have a master replica setup, your master goes down, you can bring up a replica, that's a cattle, right?
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So you have many instances, one goes down, that's not a problem, you can bring it back up.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So what we had with our initial setup was essentially a pet.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So a few issues with this.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Debugging was really hard because everything was running in the container.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: We didn't know what was causing the issue.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So a dropped packet, a dead container would show up very similarly, and we had to essentially WebSocket stream into the container to debug.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: The other issue was investigating
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: It meant we had to essentially investigating was hard because customer data would live on these containers.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So we didn't have a way in essentially to go in and debug.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So that was like the other issue we saw in our early access.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And then the last one was if a customer wanted us to connect to let's say an MCP in their VPC, it meant peering networks or shipping them our harness and having them run it.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So there were like a bunch of challenges with that architecture that we weren't able to really have a good solution to overcome.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So what we decided that we wanted to essentially decouple the brains from the hands, and I'll dive into what that means.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So the agent essentially became three separate interfaces.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: On the left, you have the session, which is essentially an append-only log of everything that has happened in the session so far.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: In the middle, you have the brain.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: That's your harness or the agent loop along with Claude.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And then on the right are the hands, so sandboxes, your MCP tool calls, et cetera.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Provisioned on demand, gone when the work is done.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And if you lose a sandbox, you just spin it back up.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So every component essentially became a cattle and interchangeable.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So when the sandbox died, the harness or Claude could choose to just spin it back up, right?
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: The error essentially went back to Claude and the sandbox to Claude was essentially like any other tool call.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So the tool call fails, sandbox fails and decides what to do and it might decide to spin it up again or choose to continue to move on.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: When the harness died, you could bring up a new instance of the harness and continue where you left off by essentially just reading your event log from the session and continue from there.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So work resumes from the last event as if nothing went wrong.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Nothing happened.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So the only thing with protecting here was your session log.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Everything else was interchangeable.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: It could go down.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: You could bring it back up.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: The other thing that we did was credentials never entered our sandbox.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: With our previous setup, your credential would be in your sandbox, so you'd be more susceptible to prompt injection.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: The change we made was if the sandbox ever needed to call out to...
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Something that needed a token or access control, it would be routed through a proxy that would inject your token before it called the external endpoint or external MCP.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: That way the model never sees your credentials or your tokens, which means you can never prompt inject Claude to say like, hey, give me your tokens or print out the tokens or write them to a file.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: You could never do that because Claude actually never sees your tokens.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: The other thing we did was because we had this append-only event log in the session, our compaction strategy could stay flexible.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So nothing is ever thrown away.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: We're not compacting and changing your event stream.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: We're always storing each and every event that happened, and then the compaction strategy is the one that's deciding, oh, do I want to look at my entire event log, summarize it and put it in the context?
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Do I want to only look at the last N events and put those into context?
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So we could have a more flexible
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: Context Strategy because of this interface design that we chose.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And then the other benefit we saw is because we could immediately start our inference calls, we were able to bring down the time to force token by about 90%.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So the Claude would only spawn the sandbox when it needed, and it would not wait for the container sandbox to spin up for you to get your first token back.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So we were able to get a much snappier and faster experience with this architectural change.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: And then here's sort of like the illustration of like one brain can reach many hands.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So your agent looper harness can now call a sandbox container.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: It could call into a customer's VPC.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: It could call into an MCP server.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So all of these like hands are essentially interchangeable and you can call and plug in many of these and it made our architecture a lot more flexible.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So if you take one thing home from this, it's that harnesses encode assumptions, and assumptions can go stale.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So we designed interfaces to outlast these assumptions and made the architecture more flexible.
speaker: SPEAKER_01

text: So this allowed us to, like I said, change our compaction strategy, change out the harness completely, but the interface and the architecture remains the same, and we can really have a more pluggable way of operating this.
